sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Any pair of inputs can be rewritten as a **common-mode** part \(v_{CM} = (v_1 + v_2)/2\) and a **differential** part \(v_{DM} = v_1 - v_2\), with \(v_{1,2} = v_{CM} \pm v_{DM}/2\). For a perfectly symmetric circuit the two parts can be analysed separately and added, since the small-signal circuit is linear. Each part needs only half the circuit.

In **differential mode** the two halves carry equal and opposite signal currents. Nothing flows into the tail, so the shared source node does not move: it is an AC ground. The half circuit is a plain CS stage with gain \(-g_mR_D\) on \(v_{DM}/2\). In **common mode** both halves push the same current into the tail resistance. The shared node then moves by \(2iR_{SS}\), so each half sees a source resistance of \(2R_{SS}\). It is a heavily degenerated CS stage with a small gain. The method depends on symmetry. With mismatched halves, or a mirror load, the modes mix and the full circuit must be used.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Inputs of 0.512 V and 0.488 V give \(v_{DM} = 24\ \mathrm{mV}\) and \(v_{CM} = 0.5\ \mathrm{V}\). With \(g_m = 2.5\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_D = 4\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_{SS} = 40\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), the DM gain is 10 and \(A_{CM} = -10/201\). So \(v_{od} = 240\ \mathrm{mV}\), while the half-volt common mode moves each output by only \(-25\ \mathrm{mV}\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Leaving \(R_{SS}\) in the differential half circuit.
- Using \(R_{SS}\) instead of \(2R_{SS}\) in the common-mode half.
- Applying half circuits to an asymmetric circuit.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The ratio of the two gains is the CMRR; asymmetric loads such as current mirrors need full-circuit treatment.
